doi:10.1016/j.apsusc.2026.167902: ABSTRACT This study presents the first investigation of the adsorption behaviour of Afatinib on gold nanoparticle (AuNP) monolayers, employing a combination of AFM–SEIRA and SERS techniques. Two types of AuNPs with distinct sizes, synthesized using different reagents, were employed to elucidate the influence of surface type on drug adsorption. The first type of AuNPs was synthesized using sodium borohydride (SB), whereas the second type was obtained using hydroxylamine hydrochloride (HH) as the reducing agent. AFM–SEIRA revealed that Afatinib interacts to the AuNPs primarily through the quinazoline ring, amide group, and amino moiety, with adsorption geometry strongly dependent on nanoparticle type. Contributions from CH3 and CH2 moieties were also identified, indicating their role in stabilizing the molecule/metal interface. Time–resolved SERS studies demonstrated that the adsorption process is dynamic and involves molecular reorientation, followed by gradual desorption, which is accelerated at physiological temperature (37 °C). Competitive adsorption experiments with phenylboronic acid (PBA) showed that Afatinib exhibits higher affinity toward AuNPs, however, co–adsorption leads to reduced stability of both species on the surface. The results reveal molecular insights into drug/nanoparticle interactions and emphasize the role of surface functionalization in efficient nanocarrier design. This work deepens understanding of adsorption at plasmonic interfaces for biomedical use.
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c03637: Here, we report the development and comprehensive characterization of copper-chitosan (Cu/CS) antimicrobial films, investigated using a combination of spectroscopic techniques and atomic force microscopy (AFM), to elucidate their chemical composition, Cu 2+ ionic release behavior, and physicochemical properties. Particular emphasis was placed on correlating the chemical and surface properties of the films with their antimicrobial performance, to relate the effects of Cu 2+ release and physicochemical properties of the films to the antimicrobial action. AFM was employed to analyze the morphology, surface roughness, and integrity of Escherichia coli bacterial cells incubated on Cu/CS films for short (2 h) and prolonged (20 h) exposure times. Time-dependent morphological changes were observed in bacteria in contact with the Cu/CS surfaces, indicating pronounced cellular stress and progressive loss of viability over exposure time. These changes included a transition from the typical rod-like morphology of healthy E. coli to coccoid-shaped cells, the formation of membrane bleb-like protrusions, increased cell clustering, and severe membrane disruption ending in cell lysis. The observed variations in bacterial morphology and surface characteristics provided a direct proof of damage to the bacterial envelope and reduced cellular viability. These findings strongly suggest a combined antimicrobial effect arising from the simultaneous action of Cu 2+ ion release (220 ppb in 24 h) and the intrinsic bioactivity of the CS matrix. The results highlight the potential of Cu/CS films as effective antimicrobial materials and support their further development for applications in antimicrobial coatings, packaging, and biomedical surfaces.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.13.751252: ABSTRACT DNA Double Strand Breaks (DSBs) threaten genomic stability, leading to cell death, chromosomal rearrangements, and cancer-driving mutations. Therefore, the effective repair mechanisms are essential for maintaining genomic stability and ensuring cellular survival across diverse organisms. At the core of this process lies chromatin integrity, which facilitates the local DNA conformational changes, regulating accessibility to repair proteins and other biomolecules. To deepen our understanding of the DNA damage response pathway, the local molecular mechanisms regulating the interplay between DNA damage formation and alterations in chromatin conformation must be investigated at the nanoscale level. Here, we integrated atomic force microscope-infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) and confocal fluorescence microscopy to explore local chemical modifications in DNA structure and chromatin integrity in metaphase chromosomes and chromosomal aberrations isolated from cells treated with the chemotherapeutic agent, bleomycin. Our findings reveal changes in secondary protein structures, indicating the engagement of DNA repair proteins with high β-sheet content. Nanospectroscopic mapping resolved the alterations in DNA condensation along the chromosomes. Moreover, we observed global DNA demethylation, particularly the conversion of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), correlating with increased DSBs. We conclude that these transitions in protein conformation and DNA methylation correlate with chromatin relaxation and enhanced accessibility for the repair protein. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT
doi:10.82444/warw.33740293: This thesis describes how electrochemical analytical techniques have been used to understand some of the physicochemical processes that underpin interfacial polymerisation reactions. A few of the reaction systems studied are currently used in the agrichemical industry for the formation of microcapsules for active ingredient encapsulation. Interfacial processes that take place at the oil-water interface of an epoxy-amine emulsion polymerisation system have been studied. Time-lapse microscopy of epoxide droplets in water or aqueous amine solutions has shown the effect of temperature on droplet dissolution and interfacial polymerisation. Quantitative kinetic data were extracted. A combination of microelectrochemical measurements at expanding droplets and finite element modelling has been used to measure the fast transfer of amine out of an organic phase comprised of epoxide and amine into the aqueous phase. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy was used to monitor a growing poly(urea) film formed at a model liquid/liquid interface at the tip of a micropipette. A simple circuit diagram was used to model the liquid/liquid interface before and after film formation, highlighting how the presence of the film will increase interfacial resistance and decrease interfacial capacitance. Poly(urea) formation under a range of different reaction conditions was investigated using a combination of impedance versus time measurements and scanning electron microscopy. Finally, the polymerisation of acrylamide monomers at a solid/liquid interface for discrete surface functionalisation was examined using a combination of scanning electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy.
doi:10.82444/warw.33738856: The aim of this thesis is twofold with both elements related to industrially relevant crystal systems and processes. The first element utilized a combined scanning electrochemical cell microscope (SECCM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) method to study the dissolution of enamel surfaces with controlled proton flux to the surface. This was then extended to investigate the effect of both known surface treatments, fluoride and zinc ions, but also a novel treatment of calcium silicate and its methods of action. The second element investigated the use of a nanopipette to investigate the early nucleation and initial growth of calcium carbonate crystals. For the dissolution of enamel, an SECCM probe to selectively etch a surface for a defined period of time with a high spatial resolution was used. The extent of the etching in the resultant pits was then monitored through AFM to measure the volume of material removed along with other pit dimensions. The method allowed for multiple independent measurements on a single sample, which could be selectively treated to eliminate comparability issues associated with measurements on multiple samples. doi:10.82444/warw.33709720: Contact stylus methods remain important tools in surface roughness measurement, but as metrological capability increases there is growing need for better understanding of the complex interactions between a stylus tip and a surface. For example, questions arise about the smallest scales of topographic features that can be described with acceptable uncertainty, or about how to compare results taken with different types of probe. This thesis uses simulation methods to address some aspects of this challenge. A new modelling and simulation program has been developed and used to examine the measuring of the fine structure of the real and simulated surfaces by the stylus method. Although able to scan any arbitrary surface with any arbitrary stylus shape, the majority of the results given here uses idealized stylus shapes and ‘real’ ground steel surfaces. The simulation is not only used to measure the roughness of the surface but also to show the contacts distribution on the tip when scanning a surface. Surface maps of the fine structure of ground steel surfaces were measured by Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) to ensure high lateral resolution compared to the capability of the target profilometry instruments. The data collected by the AFM were checked for missing data and interpolated by the scanning probe image processor (SPIP) software. Three basic computer generated stylus tips with different shapes have been used: conical, pyramid and spherical shapes. This work proposes and explores in detail the novel concept of “thresholding” as an adjunct to kinematic contact modelling; the tip is incremented downwards 'into' the surface and resulting contact regions (or islands) compared to the position of the initial kinematic contact. Essentially the research questions have been inquiring into the effectiveness of so-called kinematic contact models by modifying them in various ways and judging whether significantly different results arise. Initial evidence shows that examination of the contact patterns as the threshold increases can identify the intensity with which different asperity regions interact with the stylus. In the context of sections of the ground surface with a total height variation in the order of 500 nm to 1 μm, for example, a 5 nm threshold caused little change in contact sizes from the kinematic point, but 50 nm caused them to grow asymmetrically, eventually picking out the major structures of the surface. doi:10.1088/1402-4896/aea370: Abstract Here we present a method for the automatic segmentation of imaging artifacts in atomic force microscopy (AFM) maps collected on cell surfaces. The method is based on a U-Net convolutional neural network architecture and uses multi-channel AFM data, including height, adhesion, and restored adhesion maps acquired in PeakForce QNM, HybriD, and Ringing modes. The proposed method demonstrated high accuracy in segmenting artifact locations, as confirmed by receiver operating characteristic-area under the curve and PR-AUC metrics. The intersection over artifact, metric introduced in this work, reached a maximum value of 0.95, indicating a nearly complete delineation of areas containing artifacts. The developed approach is an efficient and scalable tool for automating the preprocessing and screening of biological AFM images, which significantly reduces the need for labor-intensive manual processing and minimizes the influence of human bias.
doi:10.1016/j.mtcomm.2026.116039: Conventional AFM morphological analyses struggle to capture nanoscale structural reorganizations that critically affect mechanical parameters such as Young’s modulus and yield strength. Here we propose a software, MechLayer Suite, that bridges this gap by autonomously identifying indentation events and quantitatively extracting elastic and plastic properties from large force-indentation datasets. The proposed software is validated using three representative systems with distinct structural and mechanical characteristics: supported lipid bilayers (SLB), monomeric and polymeric polydiacetylene (PDA), and polymer blends, covering a wide stiffness range. Differing by three orders of magnitude in stiffness, the successful analysis on selected materials demonstrates the versatility and robustness of MechLayer Suite. The proposed software enables batch processing and statistical visualization of morphological and mechanical data simultaneously, linking individual force events to macroscopic property distributions. By automatically identifying the tip-sample contact, elastic fitting interval, and breakthrough point, MechLayer Suite minimizes operator-dependent selection of the fitting region. Complementary finite element modeling (FEM) further validates the contact mechanics used for quantitative interpretation. Across the tested systems, agreement between experimental force-indentation curves and FEM predictions yielded normalized RMSE values of 0.52-7.05%, Lin’s concordance correlation coefficients of 0.9764-0.9999, and Bland-Altman biases between -5.03% and +1.77% of the experimental force range. This software establishes a new standard for efficient, quantitative AFM data analysis of thin-layer materials widely used from biophysics to polymer science.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2608.22343: Recent technical advances in atomic force microscopy (AFM) have led to the development of high-speed AFM (HS-AFM), which enables video-rate imaging and direct visualization of the nanoscale dynamics of biomolecules functioning in solution. Because HS-AFM rapidly generates large datasets, dedicated software is essential for efficient processing, organization, and analysis. Recent improvements in imaging speed have further increased data throughput, underscoring the need for faster analysis software with improved usability. To address this need, we developed Ultrafast Microscopy Exploration (UMEX) Viewer, a software suite for HS-AFM data analysis. UMEX Viewer provides an integrated environment for HS-AFM data handling, including image processing, drift correction, image and movie export, data management, and quantitative analysis. These capabilities have enabled the software to be applied to a wide range of recent studies. In this article, we describe the core functions of UMEX Viewer and demonstrate its practical applications for HS-AFM data analysis aimed at elucidating biological functions.
doi:10.1021/acs.langmuir.6c02763: We report the role of cyclodextrins (CDs) in the electrochemical grafting of the basal plane of graphite with aryldiazonium salts through host-guest complexation. Three aryldiazonium ions bearing different substituents in the para position, p-adamantylbenzene diazonium ion 1b, p-bromobenzene diazonium ion 2b, and p-nitrobenzene diazonium ion 3b, were used to elucidate how complex formation with CDs influences their electrochemical behavior and surface functionalization. NMR investigations confirmed the formation of inclusion complexes for 1b/β-CD and 2b/α-CD, whereas 3b showed only weak interaction with α-CD. The electrochemical behavior of the aryldiazonium salts was altered in the presence of CD. The grafting efficiency of 1b and 2b was improved upon complexation with CDs, as supported by Raman spectroscopy, scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM). In contrast, the effect of CD was limited for 3b, consistent with its weak host-guest interaction. We propose that CD complexation suppresses the formation of a self-assembled layer of the aryldiazonium ion at the water-graphite interface for 1b. In the case of 2b, the effect of CD complexation may find its origin in a reduction of side reactions in the electrolyte solution. These factors facilitate efficient covalent attachment. This study provides fundamental insights into the supramolecular control of electrochemical surface functionalization and offers a versatile strategy for tuning grafting density and layer structure on carbon-based materials.
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c07826: We report the formation of self-assembled molecular networks (SAMNs) by isomeric isosceles triangle molecules, dehydrobenzo[14]-annulene ([14]-DBA), and dehydrobenzo[15]-annulene ([15]-DBA) derivatives bearing six decyloxy chains, at the 1-phenyloctane (PO)-graphite interface as investigated by scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). [15]-DBA produces a Trimer+Tetramer structure with a surprisingly large unit cell comprising 12 independent [15]-DBA molecules. In contrast, [14]-DBA forms a simple Dimer structure consisting of two [14]-DBA molecules per unit cell. The lowest solute concentrations for SAMN formation are 2 × 10 -6 mol/L and 1 × 10 -5 mol/L for [14]-DBA and [15]-DBA, respectively, differing by approximately a factor of 5. Thus, even a slight modification of the triangular core shape leads to significant differences in their self-assembly behavior. Molecular mechanics (MM) simulations suggest that these differences arise, at least in part, from differences in intermolecular and molecule-substrate interactions in SAMNs. Finally, mixing the constitutional isomers results in the formation of a regular coassembly, namely a Dimer+Dimer structure. The relative stabilities of the three structures are discussed based on experimental observations and nonbonding interactions estimated by MM simulations. This fundamental information is useful for advancing two-dimensional crystal engineering at the interface.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.19.760138: Abstract AFM experiments can now produce hundreds of frames per session and this rises to thousands in the case of video-rate high-speed AFM, but every image must still be levelled to remove tilt, bowing and line noise before it can be measured. Current automatic routines rely on user-chosen masks and parameters that work for some sample types but fail on others, so levelling often remains a manual, subjective bottleneck. Here, we present two U-Net models developed using machine learning for levelling AFM images without altering the sample topography. MLMask segments features so that they are excluded from conventional plane and line background fits, and MLBackground predicts the noise and artifact background directly, which is then subtracted. Both were trained on 2,001 experimental images from multiple instruments and sample types, using manually levelled images as ground truth. On 164 unseen images, MLMask routines brought 70–80% of images below a mean squared error of 0.1 relative to manual levelling, compared with 60–70% for the best multi-plane method, with a lower mean error (0.1–0.15 vs 0.15–0.3), and both models significantly outperformed fourteen classical routines ( p < 0.01). Applied frame by frame, the models process 512 × 512 pixel HS-AFM movies at 4.7 frames s −1 . We provide afMLevel as an openly-available package for the use of other researchers. By removing the need to choose levelling parameters image by image, this package together with its models and paired training data, provides a foundation for automated AFM analysis pipelines.
doi:10.1016/j.compscitech.2026.111885: Carbon fibre-reinforced polymer composites rely on efficient stress transfer across the fibre-matrix interphase. Yet, real carbon fibre surfaces exhibit nanoscale roughness and vacancy disorder rarely captured in molecular dynamics (MD) models, which typically assume a pristine graphitic surface. This is particularly limiting for thermoplastic matrices such as poly(ether ether ketone) (PEEK), which lack functional groups capable of covalent crosslinking and rely primarily on π - π interactions with the fibre surface, making surface morphology a key determinant of interfacial performance. Here, a stochastic, Perlin-noise-based defect-generation framework is developed to produce graphene-based reinforcements with spatially correlated vacancy defects, motivated by the nanoscale roughness observed via SEM and high-speed AFM characterisation of IM7-GP carbon fibre. The resulting defective reinforcements show progressive degradation in elastic properties, with Young’s and shear moduli falling over 80% from pristine to the highest defect threshold, consistent with loss of lattice continuity. Nine stacked configurations were combined with an experimentally validated PEEK matrix to isolate the effect of surface-vacancy morphology on interfacial shear stress (ISS). The defect-free interphase yields composites with an ISS of 63 ± 4 MPa, while low-to-moderate vacancy fractions produce no significant change. In contrast, large, spatially connected vacancy clusters increase ISS by 37 − 44 %, a trend confirmed across two pull-out rates, indicating ISS is controlled by mechanical anchoring of PEEK chains within the vacancy network during pull-out. These results show that the framework generates physically meaningful defect morphologies without an annealing step, and demonstrate that vacancy architecture influences interfacial performance, guiding carbon fibre surface design in thermoplastic composites.
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c04722: Abstract Arranging colloidal particles on surfaces with tunable interparticle distances, like in non-close-packed structures (NCPS), is important for many applications. However, controlling their formation remains challenging. Although particle and substrate roughness, along with electrostatic repulsion, affect colloidal interactions, their combined effect on colloidal arrangement remains poorly understood. Therefore, model silica particles with smooth, medium-rough, and rough, virus-like morphologies were synthesized. Virus-like particle synthesis was optimized for controlled roughness (Rq = 1.4–5.1 nm) and low polydispersity (∼5%). Amine-functionalized particles dispersed in water and aqueous LaCl3 solutions were transferred onto gold substrates of two different roughnesses to form NCPS. Only the two roughest particle types (Rq = 4.3 and 5.0 nm) formed three-dimensional aggregates on rough substrates, likely due to pre-aggregation in dispersion, which could be driven by roughness-mediated mechanical interlocking. By varying ionic strength, the effect of electrostatic repulsion on interparticle distances of differently rough particles (Rq = 0.3–2.1 nm) is investigated. The rougher the particles, the less an increasing ionic strength reduces interparticle distances. At low ionic strengths, interparticle distances of rough particles (Rq = 2.1 nm) are independent of ionic strength. Smoother substrates promote lateral mobility for all particles, reducing interparticle distances more strongly for smooth particles. However, aggregation of particles with Rq = 2.1 nm remains almost the same on both substrates (Rq = 0.57 and 1.62 nm), while it increases significantly for smoother particles, suggesting that roughness-induced frictional forces are more important at short distances. These findings reveal that adjusting surface roughness can facilitate controlled particle arrangements.
doi:10.1016/j.mfglet.2026.08.076: This study investigated the effect of electrical discharge machining parameters, gap voltage, peak current, and pulse-on time on material removal rate, electrode wear rate, and surface roughness during the machining of nickel-based Hastelloy C-276. Copper was selected as the electrode material for all experiments. The experimental trials were designed according to a face-centered composite design within the response surface methodology framework. The significance of each process variable was determined through Analysis of Variance. Optimization of machining responses was achieved using the desirability function approach. Validation experiments conducted under these optimized conditions yielded relative errors of 5.6 % for material removal rate, 4.2 % for electrode wear rate, and 7.6 % for surface roughness. The analysis revealed that peak current has the most dominant effect on the machining characteristics among the investigated parameters. Despite electrical discharge machining being highly effective for machining hard materials by means of controlled electrical discharges, it often results in surface defects such as micro-cracks, recast layers, and reduced surface integrity. Therefore, the comparative study has also been performed in terms of surface characteristics of electrical discharge machining and grinding-produced parts at optimized input parameters. In the results section, the grinding-produced surface outpaces the electrical discharge machining surface in context with surface characteristics. Furthermore, a sustainability assessment using the process sustainability index indicates that grinding with Jatropha-based green fluid offers a more environmentally and socially responsible alternative to electrical discharge machining, achieving a higher overall sustainability score. Other than parameter optimization, the present work compares the EDM and grinding processes in terms of surface characteristics and sustainability performance. The central objective of the work is to evaluate the machining efficiency and sustainability considerations for Hastelloy C-276. © 2026 The Authors. Published by ELSEVIER Ltd. doi:10.7240/jeps.1904563: In this study, the morphological change of the nanofilms composed of dielectric Ca2NaNb4O13- two-dimensional nanosheets prepared via the single-droplet assembly method was investigated as a function of thermal treatment (room temperature to 450°C). The surface parameters, arithmetic mean roughness (Sa), root mean square height (Sq), Sq/Sa ratio, and slope distribution, were determined from Atomic Force Microscopy images. Based on the Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn’s tests, the heat treatment had a significant effect on the surface morphology of the nanofilms. The Sq/Sa ratio reached at 350°C (1.97 ± 0.33, p < 0.001) indicated that the temporary morphological irregularity. Conversely, the heat treatment at 450°C produced the most uniform surface with the lowest roughness (Sa = 2.75 ± 0.89) and a reduced slope distribution (mean slope of 3.15°, p < 0.001). These findings clearly indicate that the heat treatment at 450°C plays an important role in the successful fabrication of high-quality, dielectric nanofilms for next-generation nano-electronic applications.
doi:10.3390/ma19204379: This study investigates the feasibility of enhancing graphene-coated para-aramid yarn's resistance to pull-out from fabric structures, measured by junction rupture force (JRF), by increasing the fibre surface roughness with nano- and microstructures obtained by laser irradiation and graphene coating. Two types of Kevlar ® KM2 fibre woven fabrics were subjected to continuous wave CO 2 laser processing to investigate the influence of laser power and scanning speed combinations on yarn pull-out force from the fabric structure under fixed laser spot diameter and raster step. Depending on the combination of applied laser parameters, a JRF increase of between 32% and 99% was achieved for laser-irradiated KM2+440 fabric compared to the JRF of untreated fabric. Applying a single layer of graphene coating to the fabric pretreated with optimal laser parameters doubled the JRF increase. When a second layer was applied, the increase tripled, indicating that cumulative effects were produced. As a result of laser treatment, the V2KM2600_laz variant's JRF increased by 27% compared to the unmodified fabric, while the corresponding JRF difference for V3KM2600_laz was statistically insignificant, and any further JRF increase for V3 was only provided by the graphene coating layers. Meanwhile, for the laser-modified V2KM2600_laz, the JRF increase for the first graphene layer reached 56%, and adding a second graphene layer boosted it to 90%. The AFM and SEM imaging studies of the self-organization of nano- and microstructures on the surface of Kevlar ® KM2 fibres allowed us to conclude that irradiation-induced structures formed in the defect-enriched upper nanolayer of the 300-350 nm thick fibre skin, with a thickness of about 8 nm. Therefore, treatment within the examined laser parameter limits does not affect the fibres' core structure.
doi:10.1021/acs.langmuir.6c05228: Abstract Among potent psychedelic drugs derived from plant metabolites, N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) is a known endogenous tertiary amine alkaloid that can be harmful to brain activity even when present in biological fluids at nanomolar concentrations. Conventional electrochemical detection methods reach only micromolar limits, far above the physiological window, while full mass-spectrometric analysis needed for practical nanomolar detection depends on centralized medical facilities. Here, we present a three-step sensing strategy combining selective chemical activation with a self-assembled monolayer (SAM)-functionalized surface in order to facilitate nanomolar detection with extended-gate field-effect transistor (EGFET) sensors. Initially, the target tertiary amine is selectively oxidized to its N-oxide and rearranged to the corresponding amide, introducing a reactive handle absent from the native molecule. As a next step, the activated analyte is captured by an amino-terminated SAM on the gate electrode of the FET device. Finally, the resulting shift in gate surface potential is transduced by the EGFET into a detectable electrical output. Using gramine as a DMT surrogate, the fabricated sensory device achieves a limit of detection of 7 nM, well within the required physiological window. The surface-bound amount was independently confirmed by ellipsometry measurements of dried samples. This chemistry-driven activation strategy bypasses the need for complex biosensors and offers a general route to small-molecule metabolite targets that are difficult to address with antibody- or aptamer-based recognition.
doi:10.1111/idh.70186: ABSTRACT Objectives This study evaluated and compared the effects of three simulated daily oral hygiene regimens on the surface roughness ( R a ) of titanium alloy ( Ti6Al4V ) discs. Methods Twenty‐four Ti6Al4V discs were allocated to two groups based on baseline surface characteristics ( n = 12/group): Group 1 (Polished) and Group 2 (Sandblasted). Each was subdivided into three 30‐day regimens ( n = 4/regimen): Regimen A (Chemical only: 0.2% chlorhexidine digluconate (CHX) mouthrinse immersion), Regimen B (Combined electric toothbrushing [ETb] + fluoridated toothpaste [TP] + CHX after a 30‐min washout), and Regimen C (mechanical control: ETb + distilled water). Atomic force microscopy (AFM) quantified R a values at baseline and at 30 days. Data were evaluated using three‐way mixed ANOVA, one‐way ANOVA, and post hoc Bonferroni corrections ( p 0.05). Baseline one‐way ANOVA confirmed that Group 2 possessed significantly higher R a values than Group 1 ( p < 0.001). Conclusion Exposure to therapeutic oral hygiene protocols (Regimens A and B) significantly elevated Ti6Al4V roughness, while isolated bristle friction (Regimen C) had a negligible impact. Pre‐textured sandblasted surfaces exhibited greater vulnerability to structural wear than polished surfaces, highlighting the need for surface‐specific, individualized implant hygiene protocols.
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11016-2: Structural complexity in biological matter arises from molecular information that encodes supramolecular assembly across length scales 1-3 . Here we show that minimal nine-residue peptides can encode discrete lateral interaction motifs that direct supramolecular organization. These motifs generate hexagonal pores and hierarchically tile into multichannel nanofibrils with defined topology. Sequence-encoded amphiphilicity combines a cross-β-dimer, an inversion point and a trimeric junction to create complementary interfaces that couple lateral growth to axial stacking, yielding honeycomb lattices with continuous approximately 5-nm solvent-accessible nanochannels. Cryo-electron microscopy resolves the supramolecular architecture and shows that lattice symmetry and pore geometry are preserved across variants. Systematic perturbations establish sequence-structure rules linking residue position to supramolecular symmetry, lattice propagation and channel topology. Molecular dynamics simulations and vibrational spectroscopy show that the channels remain water accessible and show sequence-tunable hydration. These findings establish that a minimal, sequence-encoded interaction hierarchy can programme long-range supramolecular order, providing a general framework for how short peptides can encode complex, symmetry-defined architectures 4-12 .
doi:10.1016/j.colsurfb.2026.116252: Candida albicans (C. albicans) is a commensal member of the oral microbiota that can form biofilms, contributing to denture stomatitis. Its initial adhesion to abiotic surfaces is a critical step in biofilm formation and is strongly influenced by the material's physicochemical properties. Surface roughness, surface free energy (SFE), and salivary components play key roles in mediating fungal-material interactions. Polymeric materials are components of denture materials, so understanding the interactions with C. albicans is essential to clarify the mechanisms underlying early fungal adhesion. However, the molecular and biophysical mechanisms that govern fungal adhesion to polymer materials are not well characterized. This study examined C. albicans adhesion behavior on polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) surfaces with defined roughness levels Ra = 0.2 μm and 0.04 μm) with saliva. Surface properties were characterized using profilometry and contact angle measurements, while adhesion forces and cell-surface interactions were analyzed by single-cell force spectroscopy (SCFS) using atomic force microscopy (AFM) varying contact forces. The expression of the adhesion- and biofilm-associated genes ALS1, HWP1, and EFG1 was quantified by quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR). Rough surfaces resulted in stronger adhesion and more contact points. In contrast, higher SFE was associated with reduced adhesion. Saliva pretreatment modulated these interactions. Gene expression analyses revealed that early adhesion is primarily regulated by polymer-dependent surface signals, while hyphae- and biofilm-specific pathways exhibited minimal activation. In summary, the results demonstrate that the surface properties of polymeric materials significantly influence the early adhesion of C. albicans and its associated molecular responses.
doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15000735/v4: The viscoelastic response of phase-separated polymers systems may deviate from bulk values at the nanoscale. However, current measurement techniques lack the resolution to unmask local variations. We previously demonstrated the advantages of using a focused, pulsed infrared (IR) laser to photothermally heat a sample locally during nanomechanical measurements with an atomic force microscope (AFM), with heating controlled by varying the laser repetition rate. Herein, we demonstrate this IR heating coupled with nano-Dynamic Mechanical Analysis (nDMA). First, we measured the storage and loss modulus of a homogenous copolymer at varying IR repetition rates (i.e., at varying sample temperature), demonstrating a viscoelastic modulus response that is typical near the glass transition temperature. Further, we varied the IR laser repetition rate while modulating the AFM probe between 5 Hz and 100 Hz. With time-temperature superposition, modulus master curves were constructed through the Williams-Landel-Ferry relation, and the shift factors of IR heating-coupled nDMA curves were used to estimate the relation between IR repetition rate and surface temperatures. Lastly, this technique was applied to a phase-separated polymer blend to demonstrate the utility of the technique to decouple the viscoelastic behavior of different phases by leveraging the high spatial resolution of AFM.
doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c16183: Abstract Electrochemical processes involve transient phenomena, including nucleation and growth, phase transformations, dissolution, ion transport, and interfacial restructuring, which are difficult to capture simultaneously at nanoscale and in real time under electrochemical controls. High-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM), originally developed for dynamic biological imaging, combines nanometer-scale spatial resolution with frame times of approximately 0.1–5 s/frame, extending into the subsecond regime, enabling direct visualization of electrochemical interfaces under operando conditions. This perspective highlights emerging applications of HS-AFM in electrochemistry, including electrodeposition, nanoparticle dissolution, corrosion, lithiation-induced morphological evolution, protein adsorption, and nanobubble dynamics. HS-AFM reveals that mechanistic insight often resides in transient, nonequilibrium pathways rather than equilibrium structures alone. Advances will enable real-time nanoscale correlation of interfacial structure, kinetics, and electrochemical function.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78049-z: Polar vortices in ferroelectric heterostructures hold promise for high-density, energy-efficient nanoelectronics, but their controlled motion remains elusive due to strong pinning and lattice-coupled dynamics. Here, we report real-time observation of vortex boundary motion in PbTiO₃/SrTiO₃ heterostructures using localized trailing electric fields applied via a conductive atomic force microscopy (AFM) tip. The vortex boundaries show reversible motion that depends on both field polarity and AFM tip trajectory. By precisely steering the tip along specific paths, we achieve controlled, reconfigurable vortex boundary motion with remarkable stability over extended periods. In-situ scanning transmission electron microscopy further confirmed the controlled motion of the vortex boundary. Phase-field simulations reveal that this motion is governed by switching of the zigzag pattern at the vortex core, pinpointing the underlying physical mechanism. These results establish the feasibility of externally controlled vortex boundary motion, advancing both fundamental understanding of polar topological dynamics and prospects for next-generation polar-vortex-based nanoelectronic devices. The authors demonstrate reversible electric-field control of polar vortex boundaries in PbTiO₃/SrTiO₃ heterostructures, revealing their real-time motion and providing a pathway toward reconfigurable, low-power, high density topological nanoelectronics.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10778520/v1: Abstract Force–distance curves (FCs) are direct probes of tip–sample interactions in atomic force microscopy, but their dynamic content is often suppressed by filtering, averaging and quasi-static analysis. Indeed, in the forty years since the invention of the AFM, this hidden dynamic signal has been largely ignored, with exceptions restricted to the large oscillations associated with relatively large adhesive separations (snap from contact) or to time-averaged approaches that carry their own challenges. Using high-bandwidth interferometric detection, we directly measure fast FCs, including short-lived cantilever oscillations during snap-in, contact and pull-off. Two excitation mechanisms coexist: thermal fluctuations and transients generated by rapid changes in the tip–sample boundary condition. Cycle-resolved frequency and amplitude estimators provide time-local observables of the evolving cantilever–sample system within single FCs, creating a pixel-by-pixel mechanical-contrast channel that requires no external broadband excitation, resonant tracking or multi-pass imaging. A state-dependent harmonic-oscillator model incorporating van der Waals attraction, hysteretic capillary-bridge formation and rupture, hydration-mediated damping and repulsive contact stiffness partitions each FC into five interaction regimes and reproduces the observed responses. In repulsive contact, frequency shifts yield stiffness maps consistent with contact-mechanics estimates, enabling high-throughput stiffness mapping and localization of transient tip–sample events from individual pixels. More broadly, this hitherto hidden signal may pave the way for new ways of studying and exploiting Brownian motion in a variety of systems, providing the capability to follow time-resolved (non-)Markovian and (non-)ergodic dynamics mediated by the tip–sample interaction, including single-event dynamics.
doi:10.1002/smll.75372: ABSTRACT Ongoing advances in scanning probe microscopy techniques are continually expanding the possibilities for nanoscale characterization and correlated studies of functional materials. Here, we demonstrate how a recent extension of piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM), known as interferometric vector PFM, can be utilized for simultaneously mapping the local crystallographic orientation and the domain structure of distributed grains in uniaxial ferroelectric polycrystals, without requiring complementary characterization techniques, such as electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD). By shifting the laser beam position on the cantilever, direction‐dependent piezoresponse signals are acquired analogous to classical vector PFM, but without the need to rotate the sample. Using polycrystalline as a model system, we demonstrate that the reconstructed piezoresponse vectors correlate one‐to‐one with the crystallographic orientations of the micrometer‐sized grains, carrying grain‐orientation and domain‐related information. We establish a versatile approach for rapid, multimodal characterization of polycrystalline uniaxial ferroelectrics, enabling automated, high‐throughput reconstruction of polarization and grain orientations with nanoscale precision.
doi:10.1002/adma.75569: ABSTRACT Atomically thin amorphous carbon holds considerable promise for application in data storage, microelectronics, protective coatings, and flexible electronics. However, its device integration has been hindered by existing direct growth routes that rely on metal catalysts in contact with the substrate, causing metallic residue, film non‐uniformity, and the need for post‐growth processing. Here, we report the direct growth of monolayer amorphous carbon on a 2‐inch sapphire wafer via thermal chemical vapor deposition, in which a remotely positioned catalyst decomposes the carbon precursor into active carbon feedstock, keeping the growth substrate free of metallic contamination. X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy detects no catalyst residue across the wafer and confirms a highly sp 2 ‐hybridized carbon network, while electron microscopy reveals a random polygonal carbon network lacking long‐range periodicity. Raman and atomic force microscopy mapping confirm uniform and atomically smooth monolayer coverage, while electrical measurements establish its insulating character with ambipolar, gate‐tunable hopping transport. This synthesis approach provides precise control over thickness and uniformity at the wafer scale, enabling direct device integration of amorphous carbon for a wide range of applications, particularly as an interlayer for epitaxial growth of freestanding semiconductor membranes.
doi:10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c04262: Scaling resistive random-access memory (RRAM) toward ultradense crossbar arrays for high-density storage and neuromorphic computing requires precise nanoscale control of conductive filaments for reliable multilevel operation. Here we directly visualize and modulate nanoscale filament evolution in substoichiometric Y2O3-x thin films using high-resolution in situ conductive atomic force microscopy (c-AFM) with controlled current compliance. The switching threshold systematically increases with increasing oxygen stoichiometry, while filament evolution is continuously modulated by varying the applied bias. The initially formed larger filaments persist and dominate subsequent switching events during multicycle measurements. Using the c-AFM tip as a nanoscale mobile top electrode, single-point switching reveals localized switching with a lateral influence of approximately 20 nm, defining a crosstalk length scale. These results directly link oxygen stoichiometry, microstructure, filament evolution, and switching length scales, providing new insight into nanoscale filamentary switching and physical guidelines for scaling polycrystalline memristors toward ultradense memory and neuromorphic applications.
doi:10.1117/1.jmm.25.4.041805: BackgroundThe current carbon hard mask (CHM) film deposition techniques are not suited for mitigating x-field and x-wafer thickness and topography variation. This variability also affects both lithography patterning and post-etch critical dimension (CD) variability. Strategies to address this issue often include restrictive design rules, CHM polish, a more complex process flow. However, these solutions end up negatively impacting yield, cost, and process development cycle times. Canon’s work on nanoimprint lithography has led to the development of inkjet adaptive planarization (IAP). IAP provides planarization performance that is agnostic to feature size, aspect ratio, or pattern densityAimWe aim to collect data from wafers coated with IAP and other current available CHM-like techniques to characterize the impact of systematic local topography on the patterning process window.ApproachTopography data (AFM, Interferometry) as well as patterning data from wafers with IAP and CHM-like planarization is presented.ResultsAFM scans across 15% and 75% pattern density regions on the field demonstrated a 10× reduction in topography with IAP compared with other CHM-like planarization methods. Full-field interferometry data with ∼2.5 μm pixel size and noise levels of ∼5 nm show that IAP planarized wafers have x-field topography that is within ±5 nm. The patterning data that were collected were also consistent with an increase in the process window for the IAP planarized wafer.ConclusionsAs semiconductor manufacturing moves to more advanced nodes, CD variation plays an increasingly important role in determining whether performance and yield targets are achieved. Our data show that IAP can generate significantly flatter surfaces, which results in a wider process window, underlining the importance of controlling incoming wafer topography for critical layers.
doi:10.1002/smll.76586: ABSTRACT Antiferroelectric thin films can stabilize electrically written metastable polar states, but deterministic reset of these states after electrical writing remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that localized mechanical force can deterministically erase an electrically written metastable polar state in epitaxial PbHfO 3 thin films, driving the system back toward the antipolar antiferroelectric ground state. Electrical bias stabilizes a persistent metastable polar state, whereas once the polar state is established, tip‐applied mechanical force progressively suppresses both piezoresponse and surface‐potential contrast, consistent with force‐assisted relaxation of the polar state toward the antiferroelectric state. Time‐dependent measurements further reveal that the written ferroelectric state is intrinsically metastable and relaxes only slowly without external perturbation. Together, these results demonstrate a deterministic electromechanical write–erase paradigm, in which electric fields encode, and mechanical forces erase ferroic order. This work introduces a new modality for controlling competing ferroic phases and provides a foundation for mechanically reconfigurable nanoelectronic and logic devices based on antiferroelectrics.

doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78843-9: Abstract Repair of double-strand breaks via non-homologous end joining requires the synapsis of DNA ends. APLF is emerging as an important repair factor, capable of forming synaptic bridges in the presence of the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer. However, only a single one-to-one interaction between Ku70/Ku80 and APLF has been reported to date, which is fundamentally insufficient for synapsis. Moreover, it remains unclear how APLF-mediated bridging of Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers is prevented in the absence of double-strand breaks. Using a combination of single-molecule techniques, including Mass Photometry, Atomic Force Microscopy, and Magnetic and Optical Tweezers, we demonstrate that APLF-mediated synapsis requires threading of at least two Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers per DNA end. We show that this requirement stems from the need for a simultaneous interaction of two poly(ADP-ribose) binding Zinc Fingers in APLF with threaded poly(ADP-ribosyl)ated Ku70/Ku80s on a single DNA. We further provide evidence that long non-coding RNA NIHCOLE cooperatively binds up to four Ku70/Ku80, consistent with a synapsis efficiency enhancement mechanism based on the bridging of two Kus70Ku80s bound on both sides of the break. Our results propose a model for the physiological significance of Ku70/Ku80 threading and a regulatory mechanism based on multivalency that restricts APLF-mediated bridging to DNA-bound Ku70/Ku80.
doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c14615: Abstract Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) is a cornerstone technique for probing nanoscale electromechanical phenomena, yet quantitative─and in some cases qualitative─interpretation remains hindered by parasitic electrostatic forces coupled through cantilever dynamics. Recent approaches aim to suppress these artifacts by operating at resonance-defined null spots (NS) or electrostatic blind spots (ESBS), but their quantitative separation and evolution under realistic measurement conditions remain insufficiently characterized. Here, combining analytical beam models, geometrically faithful finite-element simulations, and automated interferometric measurements, we show that NS and ESBS are fundamentally different operating conditions. The NS is a modal zero at contact resonance where sensitivity to the selected mode vanishes for both excitation pathways, whereas the ESBS is a quasistatic position where only the distributed electrostatic response is suppressed. Automated measurements reveal that both conditions evolve with the tip–sample boundary condition yet remain spatially separated under realistic experimental conditions. While beam models capture the dominant cantilever mechanics, finite-element simulations and experiments show that quantitative prediction of near-tip behavior requires realistic three-dimensional probe electrostatics and mechanics. These findings identify NS and ESBS as condition-dependent sensing locations and provide a practical framework for advancing interferometric PFM toward truly quantitative electromechanical metrology.
